content: Dorothy Reed Mendenhall (1874–1964) was a prominent American pediatrician and the discoverer of the Reed-Sternberg cell, a hallmark of Hodgkin's disease. She completed her undergraduate studies at Smith College and was among the first women to graduate from Johns Hopkins Medical School. In 1900, she graduated fourth in her class and was awarded a prestigious internship at Johns Hopkins Hospital, where she worked under Dr. William Osler. The following year, she became a pathology fellow at Johns Hopkins under the mentorship of Dr. William Welch. During this time, she taught bacteriology, assisted in autopsies, and conducted research on Hodgkin's disease. Her most significant contribution to medical science was the discovery of the Reed-Sternberg cell, a defining feature of Hodgkin's disease. Her work disproved the prevailing belief that Hodgkin's disease was a form of tuberculosis. These findings, published in 1902, earned her international recognition, and the cell was named the Reed cell, later known as the Sternberg-Reed or Reed-Sternberg cell. Subsequently, she accepted the first internship in pediatrics at the Babies Hospital in New York, which is now part of the Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center. There, she worked under Dr. Luther Emmett Holt, a pioneer in pediatrics and the author of the first major textbook on the subject, as well as the influential book The Care and Feeding of Children. Dorothy left her medical career to marry Charles Mendenhall, who joined the faculty of the Department of Physics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The couple had four children. Tragically, their first child, a daughter, died one day after birth, and their second child, a son, died at the age of one in an accident. Their son John Blackjack Mendenhall became a renowned surgeon and later taught at the University of Wisconsin Medical School. Their youngest son, Thomas C. Mendenhall, became a professor of history at Yale University and served as the sixth president of Smith College. Dorothy Reed Mendenhall passed away from heart disease on July 31, 1964, at the age of 89.
